Turn
tûrn
v. (to change direction; to forsake one course for another; rendering Hebrew shuwb, Greek epistrepho)
From Saxon tyrnan, Latin torno, to round or shape on a lathe. In Scripture the word is almost never geometric and almost always moral: a man is going one way, and God commands him to face the other.

Biblical Definition

Turn is the Old Testament's great word for repentance, and it is a word about direction rather than feeling. The LORD doubles it for urgency and grounds it in His own disposition: “I have no pleasure in the death of the wicked; but that the wicked turn from his way and live: turn ye, turn ye from your evil ways; for why will ye die, O house of Israel?” (Ezekiel 33:11). Two things are fixed there at once. God takes no delight in the destruction of sinners, and the sinner's turning is nevertheless commanded rather than optional. The prophets press the same verb inward so that no one may turn with the feet only: “turn ye even to me with all your heart, and with fasting, and with weeping, and with mourning” (Joel 2:12). Turning is to a Person before it is from a practice, and the heart is named as the organ that must move. The covenant promise attaches to it: when a people humble themselves, pray, seek His face, “and turn from their wicked ways; then will I hear from heaven, and will forgive their sin, and will heal their land” (2 Chronicles 7:14). Wisdom issues the same summons with a promise of the Spirit — “Turn you at my reproof: behold, I will pour out my spirit unto you” (Proverbs 1:23) — which is why turning is a grace given, not a work achieved.

Webster 1828 Definition

To move round; to change position or direction; to alter in course, form, or disposition; to convert. Scripture's dominant use is moral: to turn from evil ways unto the LORD, which is repentance under its plainest name.

expand to see more

TURN, v.t. [Sax. tyrnan; L. torno, to round or shape in a lathe.] To cause to move in a circular course; to cause to revolve; as, to turn a wheel.

2. To change or alter in position; to shift; as, to turn the face to the east.

3. To alter in course or direction; to divert; as, to turn the current of a stream.

4. To change; to transform; to convert; as, to turn water into ice; and figuratively, to turn the heart.

5. To reverse; to put the inside outward, or the lower part upward.

TURN, v.i. To move round; to have a circular motion. To change sides, opinion, or conduct; to be converted; as, to turn from the error of one's way.

Key Scripture

Ezekiel 33:11 — "Say unto them, As I live, saith the Lord GOD, I have no pleasure in the death of the wicked; but that the wicked turn from his way and live: turn ye, turn ye from your evil ways; for why will ye die, O house of Israel?"

Joel 2:12 — "Therefore also now, saith the LORD, turn ye even to me with all your heart, and with fasting, and with weeping, and with mourning:"

2 Chronicles 7:14 — "If my people, which are called by my name, shall humble themselves, and pray, and seek my face, and turn from their wicked ways; then will I hear from heaven, and will forgive their sin, and will heal their land."

Proverbs 1:23 — "Turn you at my reproof: behold, I will pour out my spirit unto you, I will make known my words unto you."

Modern Corruption

Turning has been reduced to self-improvement — a change of habits, a new leaf, a better version of the same man — where Scripture means forsaking a way and facing a Person, with the heart moved first.

expand to see more

The commonest modern flattening treats turning as resolution. A man alters his routine, drops a vice, adopts a discipline, and calls it repentance. But Ezekiel's doubled imperative is addressed to men under sentence of death and offers life, not improvement; and Joel demands the heart, with fasting and weeping and mourning, precisely because the outward alteration can be performed by an unturned heart. Where the word is preached as behaviour modification, the hearer is left doing what an unregenerate man can do, and the promise attached to the real thing never reaches him.

A second corruption cuts the other way, treating turning as a change of mind only, so that a man may hold his sin and adjust his opinion of it. Scripture joins the two without apology: the wicked turns from his way, and the covenant promise of 2 Chronicles 7:14 is suspended on turning from wicked ways, not on revising an estimate of them. Recover the biblical order — the Spirit poured out at Wisdom's reproof (Proverbs 1:23) turns the heart, the heart turns the man, and the man forsakes the way. Turning is God's gift before it is the sinner's duty, and it is genuinely the sinner's duty.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew shuwb (to turn back, return, restore) is the prophets' standard call to repentance; Greek epistrepho (to turn about, turn toward) carries it into the New Testament as conversion.

expand to see more

Hebrew shuwb (H7725) — to turn back, return; the great prophetic verb of repentance, used over a thousand times and doubled for urgency in Ezekiel 33:11.

Hebrew nacham (H5162) — to be sorry, to repent; the affectional side of turning, distinguished from shuwb's directional force.

Greek epistrepho (G1994) — to turn about, to turn toward; used of Gentiles turning to God from idols.

Greek metanoeo (G3340) — to change the mind, to repent; the mind's change that epistrepho shows in the feet.

Hebrew panah (H6437) — to turn the face; the bodily posture behind the moral figure, since a man faces what he serves.

Usage

"“Turn ye, turn ye from your evil ways” — the doubled command marks urgency, not repetition for its own sake."

"“Turn ye even to me with all your heart” — the turning is toward a Person and begins inwardly."

"“Turn from their wicked ways” — the covenant promise of healing is attached to a forsaken way."
